title: Frobenius-compatible rank-one homomorphisms
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], of characteristic exponent $p$ ($p=1$ in characteristic zero). Let $(H_1,T_1)$ and $(H_0,T_0)$ be split reductive affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme], with split maximal tori, whose root data have root sets $\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ and $\{\beta,-\beta\}$ respectively. Reductivity, characters and coroots have the meanings of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]; root subgroups $U_\gamma$ and their parametrizations by the additive group $\mathbf G_a(A)=(A,+)$ have the meanings of [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Let $h:T_1\to T_0$ be a homomorphism such that $h^*:X^*(T_0)\to X^*(T_1)$ is injective with finite cokernel. Suppose $q=p^e$, $e\geq0$, and
$$h^*(\beta)=q\alpha,\qquad h\circ\alpha^\vee=\beta^\vee\circ(t\mapsto t^q).$$
Then there is a homomorphism $f:H_1\to H_0$ restricting to $h$, mapping each $U_{\pm\alpha}$ onto $U_{\pm\beta}$. For any chosen root parametrizations $x_{\pm\alpha}$ and $x_{\pm\beta}$ there are constants $c_+,c_-\in F^\times$ such that
$$f(x_{\pm\alpha}(a))=x_{\pm\beta}(c_\pm a^q)$$
for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and $a\in A$. Tori of arbitrary dimension and characteristic two are allowed.

proof.text: Apply the opposite-root SL2 parametrization statement to $(H_1,T_1,\alpha)$ and $(H_0,T_0,\beta)$. Obtain $v_1,v_0$ sending the upper and lower unitriangular groups isomorphically to the indicated positive and negative root subgroups, with $v_1(d(s))=\alpha^\vee(s)$ and $v_0(d(s))=\beta^\vee(s)$. Apply the semidirect presentation statement to both maps. Write $E_\alpha,E_\beta$ for its explicit group schemes, $\pi_1,\pi_0$ for their faithfully flat homomorphisms, and $k_\alpha,k_\beta$ for their kernel isomorphisms from $\mathbf G_m$. All hypotheses hold because each root set consists of precisely the displayed pair. No identification with a one-dimensional maximal torus is made.

proof.text: Define $P_q:\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{SL}_2$ by raising every matrix entry to its $q$th power. This is the identity when $p=1$ or $e=0$. Otherwise, the binomial coefficients $\binom pi$ for $0<i<p$ vanish in every $F$-algebra; iteration gives $(a+b)^q=a^q+b^q$. Thus matrix multiplication and determinant commute with $P_q$, so this polynomial formula is a group-scheme homomorphism over $F$. Its coordinate map fixes coefficients in $F$ and sends matrix-coordinate variables to their $q$th powers; it does not apply Frobenius to coefficients. Directly $P_q(d(s))=d(s^q)$ and $P_q(x_\pm(a))=x_\pm(a^q)$.

source.place: Proposition 23.14, printed pp.489--490, realized explicitly through the rank-one SL2 presentation of 20.32--20.33 and 21.24; formula (146), printed p.485, for the functor-of-points convention.

proof.text:
The root identity says $\beta(h(t))=\alpha(t)^q$ over every $F$-algebra. Entrywise powers therefore give
$$P_q(C_\alpha(t)(M))=C_\beta(h(t))(P_q(M)).$$
Indeed, the upper-right entry is multiplied by $\alpha(t)^q$ and the lower-left by its inverse; diagonal entries are unchanged. Using the multiplication formula of the presentations, this identity and $h(tu)=h(t)h(u)$ show directly that
$$\Psi:E_\alpha\to E_\beta,\qquad (M,t)\mapsto(P_q(M),h(t))$$
is a group-scheme homomorphism. Set $u=\pi_0\Psi$, a homomorphism $E_\alpha\to H_0$. These are morphisms of affine $F$-schemes: their coordinates are polynomials and the given torus morphism.

source.place: Proposition 23.14, printed pp.489--490, realized explicitly through the rank-one SL2 presentation of 20.32--20.33 and 21.24; formula (146), printed p.485, for the functor-of-points convention.

proof.text:
For every $A$ and $s\in A^\times$ the coroot hypothesis gives
$$\Psi k_\alpha(s)=(d(s^q),h(\alpha^\vee(s))^{-1})=(d(s^q),\beta^\vee(s^q)^{-1})=k_\beta(s^q).$$
Consequently $u$ is trivial on the entire scheme-theoretic kernel of $\pi_1$, including over nonreduced algebras. Apply the faithfully flat group-quotient universal property to $\pi_1:E_\alpha\to H_1$ and $u$ to obtain $f:H_1\to H_0$ with $f\pi_1=u$. The presentation supplies faithful flatness on coordinate rings and finite type; all other groups are affine of finite type by reductivity. Evaluating the identity on $(I_2,t)$ gives $f(t)=h(t)$, and evaluating it on $(x_\pm(a),1)$ gives
$$f(v_1(x_\pm(a)))=v_0(x_\pm(a^q)).$$

source.place: Proposition 23.14, printed pp.489--490, realized explicitly through the rank-one SL2 presentation of 20.32--20.33 and 21.24; formula (146), printed p.485, for the functor-of-points convention.

proof.text:
Let $y_{i,\pm}(a)=v_i(x_\pm(a))$. For any root parametrizations $x_{\pm\alpha},x_{\pm\beta}$ there are $a_\pm,b_\pm\in F^\times$ with $y_{1,\pm}(z)=x_{\pm\alpha}(a_\pm z)$ and $y_{0,\pm}(z)=x_{\pm\beta}(b_\pm z)$. In fact an automorphism of the affine line with polynomial inverse has degree one (degrees multiply under composition); it fixes zero, hence is nonzero scalar multiplication. Substituting $z=a_\pm^{-1}a$ into the preceding identity yields
$$f(x_{\pm\alpha}(a))=x_{\pm\beta}(b_\pm a_\pm^{-q}a^q),$$
so take $c_\pm=b_\pm a_\pm^{-q}$. The polynomial inclusion $F[z]\to F[a]$, $z\mapsto c_\pm a^q$, is injective by distinct monomial degrees; indeed $F[a]$ is free over $F[z]$ on $1,a,\ldots,a^{q-1}$ by division by the monic polynomial $X^q-c_\pm^{-1}z$. This proves surjectivity onto the target root subgroup as a group scheme (even faithfully flatness), without asserting surjectivity on the points of each test algebra. Every formula holds over all test algebras. The same argument covers $q=1$, characteristic two, and central tori of any dimension.
